headline: What I got wrong before Big 5 Construct Saudi, and how the floor corrected it
deck: Three positions I would have argued on Sunday morning, and the specific things in the halls that dismantled them.
excerpt: Before Big 5 Construct Saudi opened I would have argued that the physical trade show is a legacy format, that construction is where the Saudi opportunity sits, and that contractors are buying artificial intelligence. Three days on the floor corrected all three, and the corrections say more about the market than the positions did.
content:
Three days into Big 5 Construct Saudi it is worth writing down which of my own assumptions have not survived the halls, because a column that only records what its author already believed is a press release with a byline. Three did not survive, and what replaced them is more useful than the originals.

The first was that the physical trade show is a legacy format kept alive by habit and hospitality budgets. It is not, and the reason is specific rather than sentimental. Everything a buyer is now asked to check, build quality, finish, weight, the feel of a mechanism, whether two competing products actually differ where the datasheet says they do, is close to uncheckable on a screen. What stood out this week is how much of the floor activity is comparison rather than discovery: people arrive knowing the shortlist and use the halls to break the tie. That is a function a catalogue cannot perform, it is why buyers still touch, test and compare, and it explains how more than 1,000 exhibitors from over 50 countries can still justify four days in Riyadh.

The second was that construction is where the Saudi opportunity sits. Construction is where the attention sits. The opportunity increasingly sits after handover. The Kingdom has commissioned an extraordinary quantity of asset in a decade, and that estate has to be operated, maintained, monitored and improved for the next thirty years by somebody. Across conversations this week the companies with the most confident answers about their next five years were not the ones selling into the build. They were selling into the operating phase: facilities management, energy management, condition monitoring, spare parts, service contracts. The case that the biggest opportunity at Big 5 was operations is made at length elsewhere; here it is enough to say that I arrived doubting it and left convinced.

The award list bears that out. The show's Impact Trail gave its operational sustainability recognition to Al-Futtaim Engineering Company for integrated facilities management, which is a service business, not a product. It is a small signal, but it is pointing the right way.

Related to that, facilities management itself has moved further than I expected. The category used to mean manpower, cleaning and a reactive maintenance desk. What is being sold on this floor is asset management, preventive and predictive maintenance, building management systems, sensors, work-order platforms, energy management, fire and life safety, condition monitoring and the reporting layer over all of it. The co-located Saudi FM & Clean event sitting beside the concrete and heavy equipment halls makes more sense at the end of the week than it did at the start.

The third assumption I have dropped is that contractors are in the market for artificial intelligence. They are not, or at least not under that name. A recurring pattern on the floor was that the moment a pitch reached the word intelligence, the buyer redirected it to a number. Fewer breakdowns. Faster completion. Less rework. Lower manpower dependency. Better quality. Safer sites. Energy savings. Lower lifecycle cost. Vendors who could translate their product into one of those got a second meeting; vendors who could not got a brochure taken politely, which is what Saudi contractors actually need. That is not scepticism about technology. The visible movement is away from traditional plant and towards automation, sensors, connected equipment and machines that do repetitive or dangerous work, and robotics has stopped being a conference topic and started attaching to specific tasks: spraying, finishing, grinding, trenching, reinforcement processing, inspection. Even concrete is becoming something you can instrument and read.

The three corrections share a shape. In each case I had been reading a label, trade show, construction, intelligence, and the buyers on the floor were reading a function: what does this remove from a programme, a headcount or a maintenance budget, and will the company selling it still be reachable from Riyadh in three years. Those are the right questions, and following them for one more day is where this column ended up.
author: Mo Qureshi
seoTitle: What Big 5 Construct Saudi corrected in three days
